title: Principle 11: Change is a Must
description: Experience can be powerful — but it also can keep you from embracing new approaches or perspectives. If the old ways have worked, you're likely reluctant to challenge them. However, challenging yourself to embrace new ways will only put you in a position to get better results. Effective leaders continuously pursue new challenges and approaches that inspire everyone in the organization, including the leader, to learn, grow, and improve.

blocks.visible_title: Change Is a Must: Pat in Her Own Words
blocks.speaker: Coach Pat Summitt

blocks.markdown:
I'm constantly trying to look for ways to improve in the off-season. I promised our team, 'I will be better next year. Will you be better?' — because everyone should want to continue to improve and everyone should realize that you may have to change to get better.

— Pat Summitt

blocks.visible_title: Change Is a Must: Introduction, featuring Karen Hilton
blocks.speaker: Karen Hilton

blocks.text: Peak Performers Seek Change Constantly

blocks.markdown: Top leaders and peak performers realize that getting to the top and staying on top both require continuous pursuit of change. Growth cannot happen without change. The pursuit of change sounds really good...until we are challenged with actually thinking, feeling, and acting differently. Without question, humans instinctively tend to resist unfamiliar patterns. In a world where we seek excellence or exceptional results, however, it's important to go against our natural instinct of avoiding change. Rather, we must continuously, relentlessly, and passionately pursue it. The willingness and ability to pursue change is part of the definition of success for high-performing leaders.

blocks.text: Familiarity Breeds Laziness

blocks.markdown: Peak performers learn to loathe familiarity. If something becomes too familiar or easy, it's important for them to shake it up and make it harder. Peak performers and members of teams that become dynasties will win a championship only to return the next year with a new strategy, improvement, or approach designed to improve on previous performance. As a leader, be on the lookout for familiarity. If team members become too familiar and too comfortable, they won't perform at their very best.

blocks.text: Flexibility Wins, Stubbornness Loses

blocks.markdown: Often, being a novice at an endeavor brings flexibility to the work. A rising performer with great potential but limited experience may be willing to try a greater variety of techniques to take on the champ. Meanwhile, the champion may be less likely to try something new because, after all, they have already won the gold and know what it's like to stand in the winner's circle. This is why experience alone isn't enough. Experience with flexibility is a wonderfully powerful combination. That champion could potentially climb to even greater heights if they embrace flexibility to go along with all that experience.

blocks.text: If You Don’t Like It, Change It — The Mantra of the Most Successful

blocks.markdown: In teams and in life, stubbornness results in being stuck — a terrible place to be both personally and professionally. If you're stuck in a job you don't like or a situation that makes you uncomfortable, it can feel suffocating. High-performing leaders understand the need to embrace the mantra of change and to be willing to change virtually everything. If your job isn't what you would like, you can change it. If there are things about yourself that you don't like, take steps to change your life so you reach your personal goals. The willingness to change and the desire to improve are at the heart of what it means to be successful.

blocks.text: Take Action!

blocks.markdown: When people or teams fail to change, it's often due to "analysis paralysis." A team's members may have studied many different ways to address a problem and begin to feel overwhelmed. When there are too many choices, people tend to refrain from taking action. This is why salespeople commonly limit choices so a buyer can feel less overwhelmed and make a buying decision. An effective leader can make sure team members have choices, while keeping those choices simple. Team members must then be expected to commit to take action. Growth, change, and improvement can't happen without action. Even if team members take action and make the wrong decision, they can adjust — but those discoveries don't happen unless they take action in the first place.

blocks.text: What Are Your Limits? Change Will Tell You

blocks.markdown: The biographies of peak performers and strong leaders often reveal these individuals weren't entirely sure of their own performance limits. However, committing to change and growth often helps people solve that mystery and find out just how high is "high," or what sort of capabilities lie within. You'll never know if you could have been a great coach, CEO, or renowned performer in whatever venue you seek if you don't pursue a plan for improvement and chase it with relentless grit.

blocks.text: Change Requires Internal Shift First

blocks.markdown:
Thinking of change from Gandhi's perspective makes it quite practical and applicable. In order to inspire change in others, you have to be able to conceive of change within yourself. In other words, from within your heart and mind, do you have the ability to conceptualize change and make the shifts necessary to make it happen? Incredible entrepreneurs who want to reshape the world must first overcome their own doubts and surround themselves with people who believe their work can change the world. Companies made up of leaders and top performers who have this ability to shift and believe in themselves usually have a much better chance of getting the market to believe in them.

The willingness to experiment with change may be the most essential ingredient to success at anything.

— Pat Summitt

steps.title: Leadership Reflections: If It Isn't Broken, Fix It

blocks.markdown: So far, we've considered the perspective that peak performers and effective leaders have regarding change. They don't just wait to change or innovate when winning is in jeopardy. They commit to continuous improvement no matter what. The old adage, "If it isn't broken, don't fix it" doesn't work in a world today that innovates so quickly and comprehensively.

steps.title: From Shy Tomboy to Coaching Legend

blocks.visible_title: Change Is a Must: From Shy Tomboy to Coaching Legend, featuring Steve Olson
blocks.speaker: Steve Olson

blocks.markdown: Leaders who are committed to taking their teams to the next level must be willing to publicly declare they will take whatever action is required to grow and make necessary improvements. Without question, there is something very powerful to a public declaration. Often, someone needs to make a public declaration to make a significant change in their lives. They say it aloud and to enough people that they feel a sense of accountability to make good on their commitment.

blocks.text: You’ve Changed! Why, Thank You!

blocks.markdown: In this module, we've made it clear that it's a huge compliment if someone says that you've changed (assuming it's a positive change). If people around you notice that you're always changing, it's likely a sign of continuous growth and improvement.

blocks.text: Remember, Change Does Not Always Mean Improvement

blocks.markdown: This is not to suggest that all change relates to improvement. Have you ever known someone who changed in a negative way? Maybe they developed some poor habits or allowed some influencer to negatively change how they live or how they treat other people. Maybe it's an organizational leader who made ineffective changes just for the sake of change. Perhaps a family member fell victim to some sort of addiction that changed their behavior or lifestyle. Maybe a friend or loved one has changed in a way that causes friction or distance in your relationship. Not all change is improvement. When we use the term "change" here, we mean continuous, positive change that helps you become a better person. Your willingness to create positive change is what ultimately leads to success.

blocks.text: Aspire to Become Something New, and Love the New You

blocks.markdown: The solution here is to continuously aspire to become a better version of who you are. Visualize that better version of you on the horizon and take whatever action you need to make sure you embody all of those wonderful attributes. Fall in love with the "new version of you" that you were trying to create, and then your ongoing pursuit will become a labor of love.

blocks.text: Commit to Growing Professionally, Forever

blocks.markdown: When it comes to change, you won't always make the right decisions. You may choose to change something that should have been left alone, and you may have to change back. You may change too quickly and not embrace it for the long haul. Perhaps the most empowering thing you can do is to commit to growing, both personally and professionally, for the rest of your life. If you can always commit to learning and becoming more, there's nothing that you can't achieve. There is no shelf life on learning either. We all know there is no profession today that will allow anyone to sit idly for long without being left behind. Commit to lifelong growth and love the journey.

blocks.visible_title: Change Is a Must: Interpersonal Expectancy, featuring Steve Olson
blocks.speaker: Steve Olson

blocks.text: How High Is High? You’ll Never Know Until You Change

blocks.markdown: Could you be a CEO? If you're working in the mailroom and you don't apply for the "next job," challenging your comfort level, you'll never know. Change is the key to finding out every team member's capabilities and potential for growth. If a leader realizes the team hasn't reached its potential, they can make a change and evaluate the results. Still not there? Make a change. Getting close but not quite there? Make a change. Arrive at the top and want to stay in the winner's circle? Continue to change.

blocks.alt: image accompanying How High Is High?

blocks.text: Leaders Who Challenge You Know Your Potential

blocks.markdown: Some of the best leaders can be extremely demanding, asking a lot of everyone. It's true of coaches, CEOs, and bosses at every level. In many cases, a strong leader will see more in their team member or player than anyone else does. They may see more than the individual sees within themselves. The leader is there to help the individual find the champion within.

blocks.text: Interpersonal Expectancy Effect

blocks.markdown: In psychology, the tendency for a person to behave toward another person according to their expected behavior is known as the interpersonal expectancy effect. With this phenomenon, an individual or group's expectations for others may, perhaps unintentionally, bring about those expected behaviors, positive or negative. For example, a negative, toxic teacher may expect her students to behave badly and to be disruptive — and this interpersonal expectancy may well bring that to reality. Conversely, leaders who see outstanding things in others will remind those individuals of the emerging champions within. Simply believing in a higher level of performance in someone can help them find the next level of performance. This is an incredibly powerful element of what it means to embrace change, and leaders must keep this in mind. If you want to be a highly successful leader, think about how you see those around you and what you expect. If you are the type of leader that manages by exception, is quick to punish, and is consistently negative, you are far more likely to get those behaviors out of others. On the other hand, if you are a leader who knows how to see unexpected abilities in others and encourage them to be their best, it's far more likely that amazing people will emerge from within your organization. Have you ever noticed that some of the top leaders seem to have an amazing group around them almost everywhere they go? Sometimes this is because "great people follow great people," but other times it's because great people harvest the amazing strengths of others by the power of interpersonal expectancy.

blocks.alt: Second original lesson image accompanying organizational climate and expectancy

blocks.prompt: How might you use the interpersonal expectancy effect to inspire others to reach new heights? How might you position yourself to be the recipient of the interpersonal expectancy effect when trying to make your own personal or professional changes?

blocks.markdown: This concept of interpersonal expectancy is also powerful from an individual performance standpoint. Keep in mind that if you are a top performer, this notion of expectancy will matter. If a Division I athlete is trying to figure out which college to attend, she might surround herself with coaches or teammates with high expectations. They might want that degree of positivity around if they expect to grow. The same is true with work. This is why organizational culture is so important. When it comes to hiring, the organizational climate is one of the most important factors individuals consider when making a decision. Climates that encourage harvesting the very best from within us are far more likely to attract and keep the best people.

blocks.text: Interpersonal Expectancy and Self-Efficacy

blocks.markdown: As a leader reflecting on the merits of interpersonal expectancy, it may be tempting to assume the very best leaders have the ability to make virtually anyone into a better version of themselves. Unfortunately, this simply isn't enough. If a leader and team members recognize incredible talent within another team member, they may encourage, cajole, and push that individual, but change will only come when that person builds the self-efficacy within and believes that improvement is possible. This is inspiring, yet perhaps a bit maddening to leaders, because they can do everything right, do everything possible for the individual to find the greatness within them, and it still may not happen. Likewise, you will never achieve your highest level of performance as an individual or as a leader without a deep sense of belief in yourself. This is indeed the divining rod. The best leaders help team members find that self-efficacy within. Imagine the power of combining both interpersonal expectancy and self-efficacy!

steps.title: Leadership Reflections: Well, What Did You Expect?

blocks.markdown: We learned in these sections that interpersonal expectancy has a huge impact on the actions we take and our ability to achieve a goal. We've all met people who seemed to expect failure or disappointment and, not surprisingly, those expectations were consistently achieved. Remember, it's not enough to simply cross your arms and expect great things to happen just because you dream them. But having expectancy around positive outcomes should change both your actions and your attitudes.

blocks.visible_title: Change Is a Must: The Physics for Positive Change, featuring Steve Olson
blocks.speaker: Steve Olson

blocks.text: Change Requires Reaching Beyond the Comfort Zone

blocks.markdown: Suppose you are attempting to build muscle, but you only lift light, easy-to-move weights. Your body most likely will not respond to this comfortable — if not boring — workout routine. Instead, most trainers will suggest that you push yourself by getting out of your comfort zone, lifting heavier weights and following the routines required to take your body to a new level of fitness and strength. The same is true in virtually any other type of change. Reaching a higher level requires some straining and struggling to climb. In most cases, the higher the destination, the greater the sacrifice. To win a gold medal, Olympians must compete against the best athletes in the world who are all pushing themselves out of their comfort zones every day. The athlete who's able to push themselves the farthest will be more likely to win the gold. Similarly, a team competing in business will never grow to a new level if members don't get out of their comfort zones.

blocks.text: Why We Seek to Avoid Disequilibrium

blocks.markdown:
Equilibrium is the status quo. It's what we are used to — normal habits and patterns that allow us to pretty much keep things the same. When we challenge ourselves and add new levels of intensity to what we do, it creates a sense of disequilibrium. Although it isn't necessarily described this way in personal training, your muscles go through a state of disequilibrium when you push them with heavy weights. Once your body recovers and you have a new level of strength, equilibrium is restored. When you've reached this new level of equilibrium and you challenge yourself with even heavier weights, the disequilibrium emerges again.

Note: Your response to the following question is for self-reflection only and will not be saved or graded.

blocks.prompt: Given how good disequilibrium is for our growth, why do you think we tend to avoid it?
blocks.confirmation: Thank you! You might also save this response in your workbook.

blocks.alt: lesson image illustrating the disequilibrium reading

blocks.markdown: Disequilibrium takes a lot of energy and is exhausting. From a survival standpoint, our brains and bodies don't want to be in a state of permanent disequilibrium. If we were living in the woods, it would be counterproductive to continually have to work extremely hard at everything from getting water, to finding food, to building shelter, and so on. At some point, there are advantages to making things a little easier on ourselves.

We tend to try to avoid challenging what we already know how to do when it might permanently disrupt our equilibrium. Much like rigorous exercise can be uncomfortable (but still good for us), we might avoid studying something we know will only make us smarter. Our brains and bodies tend to avoid the hard work. However, our ability to overcome this tendency is at the heart of continually improving as leaders and peak performers.

blocks.visible_title: Change Is a Must: Wrap-Up, featuring Karen Hilton
blocks.speaker: Karen Hilton

blocks.text: Continue to Visualize Who You Want to Become

blocks.markdown: One of the most famous movie lines of all time is from the Kevin Costner film, "Field of Dreams."

blocks.text: "If you build it, he will come."

blocks.alt: From the film, Field of Dreams Photo Credit: H. Michael Miley, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.markdown: In the movie, the narrator whispers the line, "If you build it, he will come" to the main character about taking what appeared to be an absurd risk. A voice in his head told him to build a baseball field on his farm, and it made no sense to anyone except him. Costner's character had a vision for what he wanted to build and, even though there was resistance all around him, he had to commit to that vision to persist. As a leader, if you dream and visualize what you want for yourself, you position yourself to achieve the unachievable or become what you have not yet become. See it first in your mind and heart, and then chase it with your hands, feet, and energy. That is the formula for outstanding success.

blocks.text: Change Makes Us All Uncomfortable — Get Comfortable with Discomfort

blocks.markdown:
Your success as a leader or peak performer may come down to the degree to which you consistently get comfortable with discomfort. Returning to the example of exercise, if someone wants to remain extraordinarily fit for the rest of their life, they must consistently take actions that would be uncomfortable to some people. They may have to make uncomfortable food choices and do uncomfortable physical activities. Getting comfortable with these consistent, yet uncomfortable habits will very likely determine success.

It's also easy for a strong leader or peak performer to get overly comfortable with their own approaches. After all, they've already won and can reference the steps they took to get there. It's uncomfortable to make a winning coach, CEO, or peak performer change their practices to achieve the next level. How many times have championship athletes won the crown, lost a crown, and somewhat reinvented themselves to get the crown back again? Change, then, is at the heart of what it means to be a champion.

steps.title: Leadership Reflections: Are You Willing to Get Uncomfortable?

blocks.markdown: Learning yoga requires many hours of "discomfort," trying to achieve proper form and struggling to keep balance. Learning to play an instrument requires many hours of discomfort in the struggle to play fundamental scales and chords. When it comes to trying something new, many of us talk a good game but are rarely willing to actually break through that comfort zone and have a growth opportunity.
